chapter_note.about: Complexity analysis asks how the cost of an algorithm grows with the input size n. This chapter teaches the notation (Big-O, Omega, Theta, little-o), the growth-rate ladder, and how to compare odd-looking functions with logs. It then covers counting loops, logarithmic and harmonic loops, reading recurrences off recursive code, the master theorem and its failures, space, and best, worst and amortised cases with lower bounds. Almost every question reduces to one of two moves: count the work, then name its growth, or solve a recurrence and name the Theta class.
chapter_note.simple: Imagine you are asked how long a chore takes when the pile gets bigger. Complexity is the answer to 'what happens to the time if I double the pile?'. Some jobs barely change (looking something up in a sorted list), some double (reading every page), some quadruple (comparing every pair), and some explode (trying every combination). We ignore small details like how fast your phone is and keep only the shape of the growth. To find the shape, you count how many times the main step runs, using loops and, for recursion, a tree of calls. The master theorem is a shortcut for the common 'split, solve, combine' recursions. Remember that time counts all the work, while space counts only the memory in use at one moment.

cards.title: Big-O, Omega, Theta, little-o
cards.simple: Imagine two runners. Runner f may start with a head start or carry a backpack, but if you wait long enough, only their speed matters. Big-O says 'f is no faster than g, once n is big'. Omega says 'no slower'. Theta says 'the same speed, up to a constant'. Little-o says 'f is left far behind g'. Constants and small extra terms do not matter because they are swamped when n is large. In exam words: f = O(g) is an upper bound, f = Ω(g) a lower bound, f = Θ(g) both, and f = o(g) means f/g tends to 0.
cards.idea: Asymptotic notation compares how fast two functions grow for large $n$, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. $O$ is an upper bound, $\Omega$ a lower bound, $\Theta$ both at once, and $o$ means strictly smaller in the limit.
cards.definition:
$f=O(g)$: there are $c>0$, $n_0$ with $f(n)\le c\,g(n)$ for all $n\ge n_0$.

$f=\Omega(g)$: $f(n)\ge c\,g(n)$ for all $n\ge n_0$.

$f=\Theta(g)$: both, i.e. $f=O(g)$ and $f=\Omega(g)$.

$f=o(g)$: $\lim f/g=0$.

If $\lim f/g$ exists: $0\Rightarrow o$ (so $O$ but not $\Omega$); a positive constant $\Rightarrow\Theta$; $\infty\Rightarrow\Omega$ (and $g=o(f)$).
cards.intuition_full: Think of the definition as a sandwich. For Θ you must trap f between two copies of g, one scaled down and one scaled up, from some point on. In 4n² + 7n + 2, the 4n² term sets the size, and 7n + 2 is at most 9n² for n ≥ 1, so f sits between 4n² and 13n². That is why only the dominant term matters. The limit of f/g is the quickest test: it tells you where f sits relative to g in one number. A positive constant means same growth class. Zero means g is strictly bigger. Infinity means f is strictly bigger. One more picture: O is like 'at most', so n = O(n²) is true but very loose. Θ is like 'exactly this size', and is the claim exam questions usually want.

examples.setup: Let f(n) = 4n² + 7n + 2. Compare it with n² and n³ by dividing, and decide which of Θ, O, Ω, o hold.
steps: Divide f(n) by n² and by n³ for growing n. If the ratio settles at a positive constant, the two grow at the same rate.
n = 1000: f = 4,007,002, f/n² = 4.007, f/n³ = 0.004. The ratio with n² settles near 4, so f = Θ(n²). The ratio with n³ goes to 0, so f = o(n³), and so f = O(n³) too.
examples.answer: f(n) = Θ(n²), hence also O(n²), Ω(n²), O(n³) and o(n³). It is not o(n²).

examples.setup: Let f(n) = 2ⁿ and g(n) = 2²ⁿ. Which of f = O(g), f = Ω(g), f = Θ(g), f = o(g) are true?
steps: Form the ratio: f/g = 2ⁿ / 2²ⁿ = 2⁻ⁿ = (1/2)ⁿ.
As n grows, (1/2)ⁿ goes to 0. So f = o(g), and in particular f = O(g).
The reverse ratio g/f = 2ⁿ goes to infinity, so g is not O(f). Equivalently f is not Ω(g), and f is not Θ(g).
Compare with h(n) = 2ⁿ⁺³ = 8 · 2ⁿ: the ratio h/f = 8 is a constant, so h = Θ(f). A constant in the exponent as an added term is harmless; a constant multiplying the exponent is not.
examples.answer: True: f = O(g) and f = o(g). False: f = Ω(g) and f = Θ(g).

examples.setup: Let f(n) = n(2 + sin n) and g(n) = n. The ratio f/g has no limit. Is f = Θ(g)?
steps: f/g = 2 + sin n. It swings between 1 and 3 forever, so the limit does not exist.
But for every n, 1 ≤ 2 + sin n ≤ 3. So n ≤ f(n) ≤ 3n.
Those two bounds are exactly the definition of Θ with constants 1 and 3. So f = Θ(n).
f is not o(n), because the ratio never goes to 0. The ratio test is a shortcut when the limit exists; the definition still works when it does not.
examples.answer: Yes, f = Θ(n), with constants 1 and 3. The missing limit does not matter.

cards.why: Every complexity answer is written in these symbols, so mixing them up costs marks. In GATE: true/false statements about pairs of functions, often with exponentials or oscillating terms (2023 CS Q29, 2000 CS Q2_17, 2015 CS3 Q42).
how: Simplify each function: drop constants and lower-order terms.
Form the ratio f/g and see where it goes (0, constant, or infinity).
Translate: 0 gives o and O; constant gives Θ; infinity gives Ω.
If there is no limit, trap f between c1·g and c2·g (or find that no such c exists).
cards.mistake: Keeping constants or lower-order terms in a Θ answer, or reading O as a tight bound. Write Θ(n²), not Θ(3n² + 5n). And n = O(n²) is true but says very little. Also, a constant multiplying the exponent matters: 2²ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ).
edge_cases: Constants never change the class: 100n = Θ(n).
Different bases of a logarithm differ by a constant: log₂ n = Θ(log₁₀ n).
f = Θ(g) is symmetric; f = O(g) and g = O(f) together mean the same thing.
If a limit fails to exist, the definition may still hold (n(2 + sin n) = Θ(n)).

cards.title: Growth-rate ladder
cards.simple: Think of a staircase with slow functions at the bottom and explosive ones at the top. Doubling n adds just 1 to log n. It doubles n, and it multiplies n² by 4 and n³ by 8. Adding 1 to n doubles 2ⁿ, and it multiplies n! by n. So you only have to say which step each function stands on. In exam words: the order is 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ, n!, nⁿ, and any exponential beats every polynomial.
cards.idea: The standard ladder, from slowest to fastest, is $1<\log n<n<n\log n<n^2<n^3<2^n<n!<n^n$. Within the polynomials the bigger exponent wins. Any exponential beats any polynomial, and any polynomial beats any power of $\log n$.
cards.definition:
Rules for placing a function on the ladder:

- Polylog: $(\log n)^k$ is below every $n^\epsilon$ with $\epsilon>0$.
- Polynomial: $n^a<n^b$ when $a<b$. A log factor sits between: $n<n\log n<n^{1+\epsilon}$.
- Exponential: $a^n$ beats every polynomial; bigger base wins: $2^n<3^n$.
- Factorial: $2^n<n!<n^n$, and $\log n!=\Theta(n\log n)$.
- Simplify first: $2^{\log_2 n}=n$, $\sqrt n=n^{1/2}$.
cards.intuition_full: Why does each step beat the one below? Compare how the function changes when n moves by a fixed step. Doubling n adds a constant to log n, multiplies a power by a constant, but squares an exponential (2^(2n) = (2ⁿ)²). The factors by which the function grows per unit step line up with the ladder: log n barely moves, a power grows by a factor close to 1, an exponential multiplies by a fixed number, and n! multiplies by n, which itself keeps growing. A second picture is a race over a long road. A log-runner is a snail, a polynomial-runner is a cyclist, an exponential-runner is a rocket. Over a short road the cyclist may be ahead of the rocket (see the twist), but in the long run the order is fixed. So always test a big n, and distrust conclusions drawn from tiny n.

examples.setup: Put these in increasing order of growth: n², 2ⁿ, log n, n log n, n!, n³, n.
steps: Test with a big n, say n = 64. n² = 4096; 2ⁿ ≈ 1.8 × 10¹⁹; log₂ n = 6; n log n = 384; n! ≈ 1.3 × 10⁸⁹; n³ = 262,144; n = 64.
The slowest is log n. It adds only 1 each time n doubles. It goes first.
Next is n, then n log n, which is n times a very slow factor. Polynomials with a log factor sit between the powers.
Powers of n are ordered by exponent: n² comes before n³.
2ⁿ beats every power of n, because it doubles each time n goes up by 1.
n! beats 2ⁿ: n! multiplies by a bigger number at every step (n), while 2ⁿ multiplies by 2.
Result: log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.
examples.answer: log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ, n!.

examples.setup: Order f1 = n^(1/3), f2 = (log₂ n)², f3 = log₂(n!) and f4 = 2^(log₂ n) by growth.
steps: Simplify first. 2^(log₂ n) = n, so f4 = n.
log₂(n!) = log n + log(n−1) + ... + log 1 = Θ(n log n). So f3 = Θ(n log n).
A power of n beats any power of log n: (log n)² is smaller than n^(1/3). Test n = 2⁶⁰: (log n)² = 3600, while n^(1/3) = 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶.
So the order is f2 < f1 < f4 < f3: (log n)² < n^(1/3) < n < n log n.

examples.setup: For small n, is n² always smaller than 2ⁿ? Where does 2ⁿ finally stay on top?
steps: At n = 3 the polynomial is bigger. The two functions touch at n = 2 and n = 4.
From n = 5 on, 2ⁿ stays ahead (each step doubles 2ⁿ, but n² grows by a factor below 2).
Growth order only describes large n. A small-n table can mislead, so test a large n.
examples.answer: 2ⁿ is above n² for all n ≥ 5. For n = 3, n² is larger, so small tests are not enough.

Group them: polylog, polynomial, exponential, factorial.

If unsure, test n = 2^60 or take logs of both.

edge_cases: log n and √n: √n is larger for large n, even though they are close at n = 16.
n log n lies between n and n². It is not Θ(n) or Θ(n²).
2ⁿ and 3ⁿ are in different classes; 2ⁿ⁺ᶜ and 2ⁿ are in the same class.
n! and nⁿ are different: n! = o(nⁿ).

cards.title: Comparing functions with logs
cards.simple: Two huge numbers are hard to compare by eye, but their digit counts are easy. Taking a logarithm is like counting digits: it shrinks a giant product into a small sum, and bigger numbers still have bigger logs. If f has the bigger log, f is the bigger function. Powers become multiplications, so exponents come out in front, and the comparison turns into something you can see. In exam words: to compare two functions, take log of both sides and compare the logs; the one with the larger log grows faster. Use the rules log(a^b) = b log a and 2^(log n) = n.
cards.idea: When two functions do not sit on the standard ladder, take the **log of both** and compare. Since $\log$ is increasing, $f$ is bigger exactly when $\log f$ is bigger. Exponents come down in front, so you usually end up comparing simple expressions like $n$, $\sqrt n\log n$, or $(\log n)^2$.
cards.definition:
Tools:

- $\log(a^b)=b\log a$, $\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$, $a^{\log_b c}=c^{\log_b a}$.
- $2^{\log_2 n}=n$, and $3^{\log_2 n}=n^{\log_2 3}$.
- Substitute $n=2^L$ to turn $\log n$ into $L$ and powers into exponentials.
- If $\log f=o(\log g)$ or $\log f<\log g$ by a growing margin, then $f=o(g)$. If the logs differ only by an additive constant, $f=\Theta(g)$.
cards.intuition_full: Why is comparing logs safe? The log function never reverses order: if a < b then log a < log b. So the order of f and g is the order of log f and log g. The benefit is that log turns the tower of powers into plain products, which you can compare. The catch is how close the logs are. If log f and log g differ by a constant, f and g differ by a constant factor and are Θ of each other. If they differ by a growing term, one function is much bigger. That is why 2^(2n) is not O(2^n): the logs are 2n and n, and their difference n grows. But 2^(n+5) has log n+5, differing from n by 5, which is a constant factor 32 in the function. One more tip: when the logs are still hard to compare, substitute n = 2^L with a big L, such as 64, and compare actual numbers.

examples.setup: Compare f(n) = 3^(log₂ n) with g(n) = n². Which grows faster?
steps: The two look unrelated, so write them in the same form. Take log₂ of each.
log f = log₂(3^(log₂ n)) = (log₂ n) · log₂ 3 ≈ 1.585 · log₂ n. And log g = log₂(n²) = 2 · log₂ n.
Both logs are multiples of log₂ n. Compare the multipliers: 1.585 < 2. So log f < log g, and f is smaller. In fact f = n^(log₂ 3) = n^1.585, a smaller power than n².
Conclusion: g grows faster, and f = o(g).
examples.answer: n² grows faster. 3^(log₂ n) = n^1.585 = o(n²).

examples.setup: Order f1 = n^√n, f2 = 2ⁿ, f3 = n^(log₂ n), f4 = (log₂ n)^(log₂ n) by growth.
steps: Take log₂ of each, using n = 2^L so that L = log₂ n.
log f1 = √n · log n. log f2 = n. log f3 = (log n)². log f4 = log n · log log n.
Order the logs: log n · log log n < (log n)² < √n · log n < n.
Check with n = 2⁶⁴ (L = 64): log f4 = 64 · 6 = 384; log f3 = 4096; log f1 = 2³² · 64 ≈ 2.7 × 10¹¹; log f2 = 2⁶⁴ ≈ 1.8 × 10¹⁹.
A bigger log means a bigger function, so the order is f4 < f3 < f1 < f2.

examples.setup: Is 2²ⁿ = O(2ⁿ)? Is 2ⁿ⁺⁵ = O(2ⁿ)?
steps: Take the ratio: 2²ⁿ / 2ⁿ = 2ⁿ. It goes to infinity, so 2²ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ). Taking logs gives 2n against n: the multiplier in the exponent differs.
Ratio for the second: 2ⁿ⁺⁵ / 2ⁿ = 2⁵ = 32, a constant. So 2ⁿ⁺⁵ = Θ(2ⁿ).
An added constant in the exponent changes the function only by a constant factor. A constant multiplier on the exponent changes the base: 2²ⁿ = 4ⁿ.
examples.answer: 2²ⁿ is not O(2ⁿ) (it is 4ⁿ). 2ⁿ⁺⁵ = Θ(2ⁿ), so it is O(2ⁿ).

cards.why: Odd functions such as n^(√n), n^(log n) and 2^(log n) show up in most ordering questions. In GATE: order such functions or decide O/Ω statements between them (2021 CS1 Q13, 2026 CS2 Q24, 2022 CS Q11, 2008 CS Q39, 2010 CS Q12).
how: Simplify what you can (2^(log n) = n).
Take log₂ of both sides. Bring exponents to the front.
Compare the new expressions, substituting n = 2^L if helpful.
Larger log means larger function. Equal up to a constant means Θ.
cards.mistake: Comparing the exponents of unlike functions directly, or dropping a constant factor in the exponent. 2²ⁿ and 2ⁿ differ by a factor that grows, while 2ⁿ⁺⁵ and 2ⁿ differ by a constant.
edge_cases: If the logs differ by a constant, the functions differ by a constant factor and are Θ of each other.
log(n!) = Θ(n log n); but n! itself is not Θ(nⁿ).
Be careful with log log n: it grows more slowly than any power of log n.
Base 2 or base e only changes constants, but only inside a log.

example.setup: Compare f(n) = 3^(log₂ n) with g(n) = n². Which grows faster?
steps: The two look unrelated, so write them in the same form. Take log₂ of each.
log f = log₂(3^(log₂ n)) = (log₂ n) · log₂ 3 ≈ 1.585 · log₂ n. And log g = log₂(n²) = 2 · log₂ n.
Both logs are multiples of log₂ n. Compare the multipliers: 1.585 < 2. So log f < log g, and f is smaller. In fact f = n^(log₂ 3) = n^1.585, a smaller power than n².
Conclusion: g grows faster, and f = o(g).
example.answer: n² grows faster. 3^(log₂ n) = n^1.585 = o(n²).

cards.what_full:
When two functions do not sit on the standard ladder, take the **log of both** and compare. Since $\log$ is increasing, $f$ is bigger exactly when $\log f$ is bigger. Exponents come down in front, so you usually end up comparing simple expressions like $n$, $\sqrt n\log n$, or $(\log n)^2$.

Tools:

- $\log(a^b)=b\log a$, $\log(ab)=\log a+\log b$, $a^{\log_b c}=c^{\log_b a}$.
- $2^{\log_2 n}=n$, and $3^{\log_2 n}=n^{\log_2 3}$.
- Substitute $n=2^L$ to turn $\log n$ into $L$ and powers into exponentials.
- If $\log f=o(\log g)$ or $\log f<\log g$ by a growing margin, then $f=o(g)$. If the logs differ only by an additive constant, $f=\Theta(g)$.

**Worked example.** Compare f(n) = 3^(log₂ n) with g(n) = n². Which grows faster?

1. The two look unrelated, so write them in the same form. Take log₂ of each.
2. log f = log₂(3^(log₂ n)) = (log₂ n) · log₂ 3 ≈ 1.585 · log₂ n. And log g = log₂(n²) = 2 · log₂ n.
3. Both logs are multiples of log₂ n. Compare the multipliers: 1.585 < 2. So log f < log g, and f is smaller. In fact f = n^(log₂ 3) = n^1.585, a smaller power than n².
4. Check at n = 2¹⁰ = 1024: f = 3¹⁰ = 59,049 and g = 2²⁰ = 1,048,576.
5. Conclusion: g grows faster, and f = o(g).

**Answer:** n² grows faster. 3^(log₂ n) = n^1.585 = o(n²).

cards.title: Counting loops
cards.simple: Count loops like counting seats in a hall. If every row has the same number of seats, multiply rows by seats. If the rows get longer as you go back, like a triangle, you have to add up each row. A loop inside a loop is a hall of rows. When the inner loop's limit depends on the outer variable, the hall is triangular and the total is a sum, not a product. Loops one after another are separate halls, so you add them. In exam words: independent nested loops multiply; dependent bounds need a sum, and 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 gives Θ(n²). Sequential loops add, and the larger term wins.
cards.idea: To count how often a statement runs, work from the inside out. **Independent** nested loops multiply their counts. When the inner bound depends on the outer variable, **sum** the inner count over the outer values. Loops one after the other **add**.
cards.definition:
Common totals:

- Independent: `for i<n: for j<m` runs $n\cdot m$ times.
- Triangle: inner runs $i$ times (or $i-1$): $\sum_{i=1}^{n} i=\frac{n(n+1)}2$, so $\Theta(n^2)$.
- Triple dependent: $\sum\sum 1=\binom{n+2}{3}$ for `j>=i, k>=j`, which is $\Theta(n^3)$.
- Loop on $i^2\le n$ runs $\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor$ times.
- Sequential loops: $n+n^2=\Theta(n^2)$.
cards.intuition_full: Think of each statement as a point in a grid of loop variables. The loops describe a region, and the count is the number of points in it. An independent pair makes a rectangle, with area width × height. A dependent pair, such as j < i, cuts the rectangle along the diagonal, leaving a triangle with about half the area. Three dependent loops cut a 3-D box into a corner piece with about one sixth of the volume. Counting points in the region is the same as summing row by row, which is why the inner count becomes a sum. Always check the exact start and end of each loop (j < i versus j <= i changes the total by n), but the growth rate is not affected. Watch the exit test too: i * i <= n stops at the square root.

steps: The inner bound depends on i, so you cannot just multiply 6 by something. Count the inner runs for each i.
i = 0: the inner loop needs j < 0, so it runs 0 times. i = 1: 1 run (count = 1).
i = 2: 2 runs, count = 3.
i = 3: 3 runs, count = 6.
i = 4: 4 runs, count = 10.
i = 5: 5 runs, count = 15.
The total is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 = n(n−1)/2 with n = 6. That is Θ(n²).
examples.answer: 15 times, which is n(n−1)/2 for n = 6.

count = 0;

cards.title: Logarithmic and harmonic loops
cards.simple: How many times can you fold a sheet of paper in half before it is the size of a coin? Only a handful, because every fold halves the size. A loop that doubles or halves its variable works the same way: it needs only about log n steps to cover n. A loop that adds a bigger and bigger step covers the range in fewer and fewer steps: a step of 1 takes n rounds, a step of 2 takes n/2, a step of 3 takes n/3, and so on. Adding those up gives n times 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ..., which is n times about ln n. In exam words: multiplying or dividing the loop variable gives Θ(log n) runs; stepping by i inside an outer loop on i gives a harmonic sum and Θ(n log n); halving outer with a linear inner loop gives a geometric sum, Θ(n).
cards.idea: A loop whose variable is **multiplied or divided** each time runs about $\log n$ times. A loop with step $i$ over the range $n$ runs $n/i$ times, and summing over $i$ gives the **harmonic sum** $n(1+\tfrac12+\dots+\tfrac1n)\approx n\ln n$. A halving outer loop with a linear inner loop gives a **geometric** sum, $\Theta(n)$.
cards.definition:
- `for (i=1; i<=n; i*=b)` runs $\lfloor\log_b n\rfloor+1$ times. Same for `i/=b` downward from $n$.
- `for (j=1; j<=n; j+=i)` runs $\lceil n/i\rceil$ times.
- Harmonic: $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac ni = n H_n=\Theta(n\log n)$, with $H_n\approx\ln n$.
- Geometric: $n+\frac n2+\frac n4+\dots<2n$, so $\Theta(n)$.
- Square-root halving `i = i*i` or `i = sqrt(i)`: $\Theta(\log\log n)$ runs.
cards.intuition_full: A doubling loop reaches n after k steps when 2^k ≥ n, so k is log₂ n, and it is the same count either way: going up by doubling or down by halving. The exact count is the floor of the log plus one, because the first value (1) also runs. The harmonic sum comes from asking how many multiples of i fit in n. There are n/i of them. Small i have many, large i have few. The sum of 1/i grows like the area under 1/x, which is ln n, and that is the same slow log growth as before. Compare the geometric case: the inner loop's work halves each time, so the first term already carries half the total. The picture to keep is 'how much work is in the biggest term'. If the terms shrink geometrically, the biggest term decides. If they shrink like 1/i, there are log n comparable layers.

cards.title: Recurrence from recursive code
cards.simple: To find how much work a recursive function does, ask two questions about each call. How much work does this call do by itself? And which smaller calls does it make? Write that as a rule: the cost for size n equals the cost of this call plus the costs of its children. Then draw the tree of calls and add up each level. A tree with a few levels and a clear pattern is easy to sum. In exam words: read the recurrence T(n) = (calls) × T(smaller size) + (work per call) off the code, then unroll it or draw the recursion tree to solve it. Count calls with C(n) = 1 + C(children).
cards.idea: A **recurrence** says: the cost for size $n$ equals the work in one call plus the cost of the recursive calls. To read it off the code, find the base case, how many calls are made and on what sizes, and the work outside the calls. Then **unroll** the recurrence or draw the **recursion tree** and add each level.
cards.definition:
Steps to read $T(n)$ from code:

1. Base case: $T(1)=c$ (or $T(0)$).
2. Work in one call outside the recursion: a loop of $n$ gives $+n$; a doubling loop gives $+\log n$; a constant gives $+1$.
3. Calls: $a$ calls on size $n/b$ give $aT(n/b)$; calls on $n-1$ and $n-2$ give $T(n-1)+T(n-2)$.

Examples: $T(n)=T(n-1)+n\Rightarrow n(n+1)/2$. $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\Rightarrow n\log n+n$. $T(n)=2T(n-1)+1\Rightarrow 2^n-1$.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the recursion as a tree of calls. The root is the original call. Each node does some work and has children for the recursive calls. The total cost is the sum of work over all nodes. Summing level by level is easiest because every level often has the same pattern. In the example, the sizes halve (8, 4, 2, 1), the number of calls doubles (1, 2, 4, 8), and the two effects cancel, so each level costs the same: n. The number of levels is log n + 1. So the total is n times the number of levels. If the calls shrink the size by only a constant (n−1, n−2), the tree is deep and bushy, and the number of calls explodes. If the size shrinks by a factor, the tree is shallow. Whenever the tree is bushy and each call does very little, count the number of nodes.

steps: One call does n units of work in its loop, then makes two calls on n/2. So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, with T(1) = 1.
Level 0: one call with n = 8 does 8 units of work.
Level 1: two calls with n = 4, each doing 4 units: 8 in total.
Level 2: four calls with n = 2, each doing 2 units: 8 in total.
Level 3: eight calls with n = 1. Each is a base case costing 1: 8 in total.
Four levels of 8 each: 4 × 8 = 32. Check: T(2) = 2·1 + 2 = 4, T(4) = 2·4 + 4 = 12, T(8) = 2·12 + 8 = 32. In general T(n) = n log₂ n + n.
examples.answer: T(8) = 32, and T(n) = n log₂ n + n = Θ(n log n).

Each call spawns two calls of sizes only 2 and 3 smaller, so the tree widens: the number of calls grows exponentially (about 1.32ⁿ).
examples.answer: 13 calls; exponential growth.

cards.mistake: Counting the work of a loop as n when it doubles (log n), or forgetting that two recursive calls double the calls. Read the loop bound carefully, and count each call in the tree separately.
edge_cases: Two calls on n−1 give about 2ⁿ calls; two calls on n/2 give about n calls.

Steps to read $T(n)$ from code:

1. Base case: $T(1)=c$ (or $T(0)$).
2. Work in one call outside the recursion: a loop of $n$ gives $+n$; a doubling loop gives $+\log n$; a constant gives $+1$.
3. Calls: $a$ calls on size $n/b$ give $aT(n/b)$; calls on $n-1$ and $n-2$ give $T(n-1)+T(n-2)$.

Examples: $T(n)=T(n-1)+n\Rightarrow n(n+1)/2$. $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n\Rightarrow n\log n+n$. $T(n)=2T(n-1)+1\Rightarrow 2^n-1$.

**Worked example.** Read off the recurrence and find the total work for n = 8.
```c
void w(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return;       // costs 1
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++)   // n units of work
        work();
    w(n / 2);
    w(n / 2);
}
```

1. One call does n units of work in its loop, then makes two calls on n/2. So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, with T(1) = 1.
2. Level 0: one call with n = 8 does 8 units of work.
3. Level 1: two calls with n = 4, each doing 4 units: 8 in total.
4. Level 2: four calls with n = 2, each doing 2 units: 8 in total.
5. Level 3: eight calls with n = 1. Each is a base case costing 1: 8 in total.
6. Four levels of 8 each: 4 × 8 = 32. Check: T(2) = 2·1 + 2 = 4, T(4) = 2·4 + 4 = 12, T(8) = 2·12 + 8 = 32. In general T(n) = n log₂ n + n.

**Answer:** T(8) = 32, and T(n) = n log₂ n + n = Θ(n log n).

cards.title: Master theorem
cards.simple: A divide-and-conquer algorithm splits a job into smaller jobs and combines the answers. Picture the tree of jobs: one big combining job at the top and many tiny jobs at the bottom. The master theorem asks who wins, the top, the bottom, or neither. If the tiny jobs at the bottom do the most work, the answer is the number of leaves. If every level costs the same, you pay that cost once per level. If the top job swamps the rest, the answer is its combining work. In exam words: for T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), compare f(n) with n^(log_b a); smaller gives Θ(n^(log_b a)), equal adds a log n, and larger gives Θ(f(n)).
cards.idea: For $T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)$, compare $f(n)$ with the **critical power** $n^c$, where $c=\log_b a$ (the number of leaves is about $n^c$). Polynomially smaller: leaves win, $\Theta(n^c)$. Equal: $\Theta(n^c\log n)$. Polynomially larger: the root wins, $\Theta(f(n))$.
cards.definition:
Let $a\ge1$, $b>1$, $c=\log_b a$:

1. $f(n)=O(n^{c-\epsilon})$ for some $\epsilon>0$: $T(n)=\Theta(n^{c})$.
2. $f(n)=\Theta(n^{c})$: $T(n)=\Theta(n^{c}\log n)$.
3. $f(n)=\Omega(n^{c+\epsilon})$ and $af(n/b)\le kf(n)$ for some $k<1$: $T(n)=\Theta(f(n))$.

The gap must be a **polynomial** factor $n^\epsilon$. A log factor is not enough.
cards.intuition_full: Draw the tree. Level k has $a^k$ calls, each of size $n/b^k$, so the level costs $a^k f(n/b^k)$. The leaves number $a^{\log_b n}=n^{c}$. In case 1 the level costs grow geometrically as you go down, so the sum is a geometric series dominated by its last term, the leaves. In case 2 every level costs the same, and there are about $\log_b n$ levels. In case 3 the level costs shrink geometrically as you go down, so the first term (the root) dominates. That is all the theorem says, and the picture explains why the polynomial gap matters: a log factor does not make the series geometric, so no term dominates. Also check that the recurrence has the right form: $a$ must be a constant at least 1, the subproblem size must be $n/b$, and $f$ must be reasonable. For anything else, use the tree.

examples.setup: Solve T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n² with the master theorem, and check with T(16) (take T(1) = 1).
steps: Read the parameters: a = 8 calls, each on size n/2, so b = 2, and the work outside is f(n) = n².
The critical power is n^c with c = log_b a = log₂ 8 = 3. Compare f(n) = n² with n³: f is smaller by a full factor of n, which is polynomially smaller. This is case 1: the leaves dominate.
Check with the tree for n = 16. Level k costs 8ᵏ · (16/2ᵏ)² = 256 · 2ᵏ: that is 256, 512, 1024, 2048 for levels 0 to 3.
The 4096 leaves (8⁴) cost 1 each, so the last level costs 4096. The cost doubles each level, so the bottom level carries about half of everything.
examples.answer: T(n) = Θ(n³), since f(n) = n² is polynomially smaller than n^(log₂ 8) = n³.

examples.setup: Solve T(n) = 16T(n/4) + n². Then solve T(n) = 7T(n/2) + n².

examples.setup: Try the master theorem on T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n log n. Which case applies?
steps: a = 2, b = 2, so c = 1 and n^c = n. Here f(n) = n log n is larger than n.

examples.answer: The basic master theorem does not apply (a gap of only log n). T(n) = Θ(n log² n).

cards.title: Beyond the master theorem
cards.simple: Some recurrences do not fit the neat 'split into equal parts' shape, so the master theorem cannot be used. Three tricks cover almost all of them. For a sum like T(n−1) + n, just add the terms. For a square root, notice that taking √n halves the number of digits in the exponent, so you count halvings of the exponent, which is a log of a log. For unequal splits, draw the recursion tree and bound it between its shallowest and deepest branch. In exam words: for T(n−1) + n unroll and sum; for T(√n) substitute n = 2^m so the recurrence becomes S(m) = S(m/2) + 1; for unequal splits use the recursion tree; and when f(n) differs from n^c by only a log factor, use the tree too.
cards.idea: When the master theorem does not apply, **unroll** and sum, **substitute** $n=2^m$ to turn square roots into halvings, or use the **recursion tree** to bound unequal splits. The usual results: $T(n-1)+n\to\Theta(n^2)$, $T(\sqrt n)+1\to\Theta(\log\log n)$, and $2T(n-1)+c\to\Theta(2^n)$.
cards.definition:
- $T(n)=T(n-1)+f(n)$: $T(n)=T(0)+\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(k)$. With $f=n$: $n(n+1)/2$.
- $T(n)=T(\sqrt n)+1$: put $n=2^m$, $S(m)=T(2^m)=S(m/2)+1$, so $S=\Theta(\log m)$ and $T=\Theta(\log\log n)$.
- $T(n)=2T(\sqrt n)+\log n$: $S(m)=2S(m/2)+m$ gives $\Theta(m\log m)$, so $T=\Theta(\log n\,\log\log n)$.
- Unequal splits $T(\alpha n)+T((1-\alpha)n)+n$: every level costs at most $n$ and the depth is $\Theta(\log n)$, so $\Theta(n\log n)$.
- $T(n)=aT(n-1)+f$ with $a\ge2$: exponential $\Theta(a^n)$.
- $T(n)=2T(n/2)+n/\log n$: levels cost $n/(\log n-k)$, total $\Theta(n\log\log n)$.
cards.intuition_full: These all come from the same habit: ask how many levels the recursion has, and what each level costs. For T(n−1) + n, there are n levels and the level costs 1, 2, ..., n, whose sum is quadratic. For √n, each call keeps only half of the digits of the exponent, so after k calls the exponent has been divided by 2ᵏ. The recursion ends when it reaches a constant, which takes log m steps, where m is the exponent itself. That is why it is log log n. For unequal splits, the tree has branches of different lengths, but every level that is full costs exactly n. Since the shallow branch has about log n levels and the deep branch also has about log n levels (with a different base, which is a constant factor), the total is n log n. For exponential recurrences, the number of calls doubles per level while the depth is n, so the leaf count is 2ⁿ. A reliable check for any answer is to compute the first few values and compare with the claimed closed form.

examples.setup: Solve T(n) = T(√n) + 1 with T(2) = 1. How many calls does n = 65536 make?
steps: The master theorem does not fit, because √n is not n/b. Substitute n = 2^m, so m = log₂ n. For n = 65536, m = 16.
One call reduces n to √n = 256 = 2⁸. In terms of the exponent, m goes from 16 to 8: the exponent halves.
256 reduces to √256 = 16 = 2⁴, so m = 4.
16 reduces to 4 (m = 2), then 4 reduces to 2 (m = 1), where the base case T(2) stops it. The chain is 65536, 256, 16, 4, 2: five calls.
The exponent halved 4 times, and 16 = 2⁴, so the number of halvings is log₂ 16 = log₂ log₂ n. Hence T(n) = Θ(log log n).
examples.answer: 5 calls for n = 65536. In general T(n) = Θ(log log n).

examples.setup: Solve T(n) = T(n/5) + T(4n/5) + n, which has unequal splits.
steps: The two pieces always add up to n, so every full level of the recursion tree costs exactly n.
The shallow branch (always n/5) reaches size 1 after log₅ n levels. The deep branch (always 4n/5) lasts log_{5/4} n levels.
All levels down to the shallow depth cost n each, so T(n) ≥ n log₅ n. No level ever costs more than n, so T(n) ≤ n log_{5/4} n.
Both bounds are constant multiples of n log n, so T(n) = Θ(n log n).
Numerical check: for n = 10⁶ the recurrence gives T(n) ≈ 2.88 × 10⁷, and n log₂ n ≈ 1.99 × 10⁷, a ratio of about 1.44.
examples.answer: T(n) = Θ(n log n). Bound the tree between its shallowest and deepest branches.

examples.setup: Solve T(n) = 2T(n−1) + n with T(1) = 1. Find the closed form.
steps: Each step doubles the previous value, so the growth is exponential. The solution has the form A·2ⁿ + (a linear part).

cards.title: Space complexity
cards.simple: Think of desk space. The input is already on your desk, and auxiliary space is the extra table you must borrow. Copying 1000 papers needs room for 1000 more. Swapping papers in place needs room for just the one paper in your hand. A recursive helper is different: each unfinished call is a sticky note on the desk, so a chain of 1000 unfinished calls needs 1000 notes. In exam words: auxiliary space is extra memory beyond the input; a recursion of depth d uses Θ(d) stack space; time counts all calls, but space counts only the deepest chain alive at once.
cards.idea: **Auxiliary space** is the extra memory an algorithm uses beyond its input. Variables and indices cost $O(1)$, a copy of the input costs $\Theta(n)$, and each active recursive call costs a stack frame, so a recursion of depth $d$ costs $\Theta(d)$. Time counts every call; space counts only the longest chain alive together.
cards.definition:
Common cases:

- Running sum, counters, swaps: $O(1)$.
- Copying or building a new array of size $n$: $\Theta(n)$.
- Recursion with depth $d$ (one call alive per level): $\Theta(d)$.
- Binary search recursion or halving recursion: $\Theta(\log n)$ stack.
- Linear recursion `f(n-1)`: $\Theta(n)$ stack.
- Merge sort: $\Theta(n)$ extra; quicksort: $\Theta(\log n)$ expected, $\Theta(n)$ worst case; heapsort: $O(1)$.
- The input itself is not counted unless the question says 'total space'.
cards.intuition_full: Time and space measure different things. Time adds up the work of every call, so the number of calls matters. Space is a memory peak: how much is in use at one moment. When calls run one after another, the first has finished and been popped before the second starts, so the memory is reused. Only nested calls (a call inside a call) stack up. That is why a tree with 2047 calls can have a stack of only 11 frames: its depth is only 11. A second picture is a chain of dominoes against a bushy tree. A chain of n calls needs n frames. A balanced tree of n calls needs only log n frames. In-place algorithms avoid copies: they rearrange the input using a few scratch cells. Whenever a question says 'extra space', ask what it copies and how deep it recurses.

examples.setup: Two ways to reverse the array `a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]` (n = 8). What is the auxiliary space of each?
steps: The array has n = 8 elements. The goal is `[6, 2, 9, 5, 1, 4, 1, 3]`. Auxiliary space means extra memory beyond the input.
Method A: make a new array b of 8 cells and copy from the end of a into b. That is n extra cells: Θ(n) space.
Method B (in place): two indices i = 0 and j = 7. Swap a[0] and a[7] using one temporary cell. The array becomes `6 1 4 1 5 9 2 3`.
Move inwards: i = 1, j = 6. Swap: `6 2 4 1 5 9 1 3`.
i = 2, j = 5: swap, giving `6 2 9 1 5 4 1 3`. Then i = 3, j = 4: swap, giving `6 2 9 5 1 4 1 3`. Done.
Method B used only i, j and one temp: 3 cells, whatever n is. That is O(1) auxiliary space. Both methods take Θ(n) time.
examples.answer: Method A: Θ(n) auxiliary space. Method B: O(1). The time is Θ(n) for both.

steps: Time: count calls. C(n) = 1 + 2C(n/2), C(1) = 1. That gives C(1024) = 2·1024 − 1 = 2047 calls, so the time is Θ(n).
Space: the two calls run one after the other, not at the same time. At any moment, only one chain of nested calls is alive.
The longest chain is 1024, 512, 256, ..., 2, 1: 11 frames, which is log₂ 1024 + 1.
So the stack space is Θ(log n), far below the number of calls.
examples.answer: Time Θ(n) (2047 calls). Auxiliary space Θ(log n) (11 frames at most).

examples.setup: Quicksort uses the first element as the pivot and recurses on both sides. What stack depth does it reach on the sorted input 1, 2, ..., 7 and on a balanced input like 4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7?
steps: Sorted input: the pivot 1 leaves nothing on the left and 6 elements on the right. The next pivot 2 leaves 5, and so on. The recursion goes 7 levels deep.
Balanced input: the pivot 4 splits 3 and 3, and each half splits again. The recursion goes 3 levels deep.
So the auxiliary stack space is Θ(n) in the worst case and Θ(log n) in the best. The usual fix is to recurse into the smaller side first.
examples.answer: 7 frames for the sorted input (Θ(n) worst case) and 3 frames for the balanced input (Θ(log n)).

example.setup: Two ways to reverse the array `a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]` (n = 8). What is the auxiliary space of each?

cards.what_full:
**Auxiliary space** is the extra memory an algorithm uses beyond its input. Variables and indices cost $O(1)$, a copy of the input costs $\Theta(n)$, and each active recursive call costs a stack frame, so a recursion of depth $d$ costs $\Theta(d)$. Time counts every call; space counts only the longest chain alive together.

Common cases:

- Running sum, counters, swaps: $O(1)$.
- Copying or building a new array of size $n$: $\Theta(n)$.
- Recursion with depth $d$ (one call alive per level): $\Theta(d)$.
- Binary search recursion or halving recursion: $\Theta(\log n)$ stack.
- Linear recursion `f(n-1)`: $\Theta(n)$ stack.
- Merge sort: $\Theta(n)$ extra; quicksort: $\Theta(\log n)$ expected, $\Theta(n)$ worst case; heapsort: $O(1)$.
- The input itself is not counted unless the question says 'total space'.

**Worked example.** Two ways to reverse the array `a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]` (n = 8). What is the auxiliary space of each?

1. The array has n = 8 elements. The goal is `[6, 2, 9, 5, 1, 4, 1, 3]`. Auxiliary space means extra memory beyond the input.
2. Method A: make a new array b of 8 cells and copy from the end of a into b. That is n extra cells: Θ(n) space.
3. Method B (in place): two indices i = 0 and j = 7. Swap a[0] and a[7] using one temporary cell. The array becomes `6 1 4 1 5 9 2 3`.
4. Move inwards: i = 1, j = 6. Swap: `6 2 4 1 5 9 1 3`.
5. i = 2, j = 5: swap, giving `6 2 9 1 5 4 1 3`. Then i = 3, j = 4: swap, giving `6 2 9 5 1 4 1 3`. Done.
6. Method B used only i, j and one temp: 3 cells, whatever n is. That is O(1) auxiliary space. Both methods take Θ(n) time.

**Answer:** Method A: Θ(n) auxiliary space. Method B: O(1). The time is Θ(n) for both.

cards.title: Cases, amortisation and lower bounds
cards.simple: The same algorithm can be fast on one input and slow on another. Searching for a name in an unsorted list takes one look if it is first and a full scan if it is last. That gives a best case, a worst case and an average case. Sometimes a single step is expensive but happens rarely, like a bus that sometimes stops for a long break. Averaging over a whole run gives the amortised cost. And sometimes you can prove that no method can beat a certain number of steps, a lower bound, as in 'at least 7 comparisons to sort 5 items'. In exam words: best, worst and average case describe different inputs; amortised cost is total work divided by the number of operations; lower bounds count what any algorithm must do, such as ceil(3n/2) − 2 for min and max.
cards.idea: **Best, worst and average case** describe the same algorithm on different inputs. **Amortised cost** is the total work of a sequence divided by the number of operations. A **lower bound** says every algorithm needs at least this much, usually proved by counting outcomes or by an adversary argument.
cards.definition:
Useful results:

- Linear search: best $1$, worst $n$, average $(n+1)/2$ (key present, uniform).
- Max and min together: $\lceil 3n/2\rceil-2$ comparisons (pair up), better than $2(n-1)$.
- Second largest with a tournament: $n+\lceil\log_2 n\rceil-2$ comparisons.
- Binary counter, $n$ increments: at most $2n$ bit flips, so $O(1)$ amortised. Doubling array: $O(1)$ amortised append.
- Comparison sort lower bound: $\lceil\log_2 n!\rceil=\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons.
- Any non-maximum is known after one comparison where it loses.
cards.intuition_full: Amortised analysis balances rare expensive operations against many cheap ones. In a doubling array, the copy before the 9th append costs 8, but it pays for the next 8 free appends. Spread it out, and each append is charged a small constant. This is not an average over random inputs; it is a guarantee on any sequence. Lower bounds come from the other direction. A comparison sort gives one bit of information per comparison, so with k comparisons it can tell apart at most 2^k outcomes. There are n! orderings, so you need 2^k ≥ n!, hence k ≥ log₂ n!. For max and min, pairing works because a loser cannot be the maximum and a winner cannot be the minimum, so each element only needs to be compared in one of the two contests. The same thinking, who can still be the answer, drives most exam questions of this kind.

examples.setup: Find both the maximum and the minimum of `17 4 29 8 11 23 2 15 31 6` (n = 10) with as few comparisons as possible.
steps: The plain method (find the max with 9 comparisons, then the min with 9) costs 2(n − 1) = 18 comparisons.
Pair the numbers and compare each pair: (17,4), (29,8), (11,23), (2,15), (31,6). That is 5 comparisons. The winners are 17, 29, 23, 15, 31 and the losers are 4, 8, 11, 2, 6.
The maximum must be a winner (a loser lost to someone bigger). Find the max of the 5 winners with 4 comparisons: 31.
The minimum must be a loser. Find the min of the 5 losers with 4 comparisons: 2.
Total: 5 + 4 + 4 = 13 = ceil(3n/2) − 2 = 15 − 2. That is fewer than 18, and 13 is also a lower bound.
examples.answer: Max 31, min 2, using 13 comparisons = ceil(3n/2) − 2.

examples.setup: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full (copying every element). It receives 9 appends. What is the total work, and the amortised cost per append?
steps: Each append writes 1 element: 9 writes in total.
The array is full, so it copies and doubles, before appends 2, 3, 5 and 9. The copies are 1, 2, 4 and 8 elements.
Total copies: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. Total work: 9 + 15 = 24.
Amortised cost: 24 / 9 ≈ 2.7 per append, a constant. In general the copies sum to less than 2n, so the amortised cost is O(1), although a single append can cost O(n).
examples.answer: 24 operations in total, about 2.7 per append: O(1) amortised.

examples.setup: Can 5 distinct numbers be sorted with 6 comparisons in the worst case?
steps: A comparison-based sort is a binary decision tree. Each of the 5! = 120 orderings needs its own leaf.
A tree with 6 comparisons on every path has at most 2⁶ = 64 leaves.
64 < 120, so some orderings would share a leaf. Impossible.
The lower bound is ceil(log₂ 120) = 7 comparisons. (Seven are enough, by a careful method.)
examples.answer: No. At least ceil(log₂ 5!) = 7 comparisons are needed in the worst case.

cards.why: These are the 'think before you code' questions: what must any algorithm do, and what does it cost on average. In GATE: min-max comparison counts (2021 CS1 Q12, 2014 CS1 Q39, 2007 CS Q50), amortised cost of a counter (2004 CS Q82), and small lower-bound arguments (2025 CS2 Q20, 2024 CS1 Q17, 2015 CS2 Q22).
how: Decide what is asked: best, worst, average, amortised or a lower bound.
For min and max together, use pairing: ceil(3n/2) − 2.
For amortised cost, total the work over the whole sequence and divide by the number of operations.
For a lower bound, count the outcomes to tell apart and use a decision tree: at least ceil(log₂ outcomes).
cards.mistake: Mixing amortised cost with average case, or applying the 2(n − 1) plain count to the min-max problem. Amortised is a worst-case guarantee over a sequence. The average case needs a probability model.
edge_cases: n = 1: min and max need 0 comparisons.
Odd n: one element is left unpaired, which still costs ceil(3n/2) − 2 in total.
A single doubling append costs O(n), but the sequence total is O(n).
Average case needs a stated input distribution; 'average' without one is not defined.

scenes.title: f(n) = 4n^2 + 7n + 2: the ratio with n^2 settles, the ratio with n^3 vanishes

steps.caption: Divide f(n) by n² and by n³ for growing n. If the ratio settles at a positive constant, the two grow at the same rate.
n = 1000: f = 4,007,002, f/n² = 4.007, f/n³ = 0.004. The ratio with n² settles near 4, so f = Θ(n²). The ratio with n³ goes to 0, so f = o(n³), and so f = O(n³) too.

scenes.title: Sorting the growth ladder at n = 64

objects.label: slowest at the left, fastest at the right

steps.caption: Test with a big n, say n = 64. n² = 4096; 2ⁿ ≈ 1.8 × 10¹⁹; log₂ n = 6; n log n = 384; n! ≈ 1.3 × 10⁸⁹; n³ = 262,144; n = 64.
The slowest is log n. It adds only 1 each time n doubles. It goes first.

set.text: log n = 6 : adds 1 when n doubles

steps.caption: Next is n, then n log n, which is n times a very slow factor. Polynomials with a log factor sit between the powers.
Powers of n are ordered by exponent: n² comes before n³.
2ⁿ beats every power of n, because it doubles each time n goes up by 1.

set.text: 2^n doubles per step: beats every power

steps.caption: n! beats 2ⁿ: n! multiplies by a bigger number at every step (n), while 2ⁿ multiplies by 2.

set.text: n! multiplies by n per step: beats 2^n

steps.caption: Result: log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.

set.text: log n < n < nlogn < n^2 < n^3 < 2^n < n!

scenes.title: Compare odd functions by taking logs of both sides

steps.caption: The two look unrelated, so write them in the same form. Take log₂ of each.
log f = log₂(3^(log₂ n)) = (log₂ n) · log₂ 3 ≈ 1.585 · log₂ n. And log g = log₂(n²) = 2 · log₂ n.
Both logs are multiples of log₂ n. Compare the multipliers: 1.585 < 2. So log f < log g, and f is smaller. In fact f = n^(log₂ 3) = n^1.585, a smaller power than n².
Conclusion: g grows faster, and f = o(g).
The inner bound depends on i, so you cannot just multiply 6 by something. Count the inner runs for each i.
i = 0: the inner loop needs j < 0, so it runs 0 times. i = 1: 1 run (count = 1).
i = 2: 2 runs, count = 3.
i = 3: 3 runs, count = 6.
i = 4: 4 runs, count = 10.
i = 5: 5 runs, count = 15.
The total is 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15 = n(n−1)/2 with n = 6. That is Θ(n²).

scenes.title: A loop that multiplies i by 3: 1, 3, 9, 27, 81 pass, 243 stops it

objects.label: values of i that pass i <= 100

steps.caption: The loop variable is multiplied by 3 each time, so it does not step through every number. Write the values of i that pass the test i ≤ 100.

set.text: i is multiplied by 3 each time

steps.caption: i = 1 passes: run 1.
i = 3 passes: run 2. i = 9 passes: run 3.
i = 27 passes: run 4. i = 81 passes: run 5.
Next i = 243 fails 243 ≤ 100, so the loop stops. count = 5 = floor(log₃ 100) + 1 = 4 + 1.

scenes.title: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n for n = 8: every level costs 8

steps.caption: One call does n units of work in its loop, then makes two calls on n/2. So T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n, with T(1) = 1.
Level 0: one call with n = 8 does 8 units of work.
Level 1: two calls with n = 4, each doing 4 units: 8 in total.
Level 2: four calls with n = 2, each doing 2 units: 8 in total.
Level 3: eight calls with n = 1. Each is a base case costing 1: 8 in total.
Four levels of 8 each: 4 × 8 = 32. Check: T(2) = 2·1 + 2 = 4, T(4) = 2·4 + 4 = 12, T(8) = 2·12 + 8 = 32. In general T(n) = n log₂ n + n.

scenes.title: T(n) = 8T(n/2) + n^2 at n = 16: the work doubles at every level

steps.caption: Read the parameters: a = 8 calls, each on size n/2, so b = 2, and the work outside is f(n) = n².
The critical power is n^c with c = log_b a = log₂ 8 = 3. Compare f(n) = n² with n³: f is smaller by a full factor of n, which is polynomially smaller. This is case 1: the leaves dominate.

set.text: f(n) = n^2 is smaller than n^3 : case 1

steps.caption: Check with the tree for n = 16. Level k costs 8ᵏ · (16/2ᵏ)² = 256 · 2ᵏ: that is 256, 512, 1024, 2048 for levels 0 to 3.
The 4096 leaves (8⁴) cost 1 each, so the last level costs 4096. The cost doubles each level, so the bottom level carries about half of everything.

set.text: 4096 leaves x cost 1 : bottom level dominates

scenes.title: T(n) = T(sqrt n) + 1: the exponent log n halves at every call

steps.caption: The master theorem does not fit, because √n is not n/b. Substitute n = 2^m, so m = log₂ n. For n = 65536, m = 16.
One call reduces n to √n = 256 = 2⁸. In terms of the exponent, m goes from 16 to 8: the exponent halves.
256 reduces to √256 = 16 = 2⁴, so m = 4.
16 reduces to 4 (m = 2), then 4 reduces to 2 (m = 1), where the base case T(2) stops it. The chain is 65536, 256, 16, 4, 2: five calls.
The exponent halved 4 times, and 16 = 2⁴, so the number of halvings is log₂ 16 = log₂ log₂ n. Hence T(n) = Θ(log log n).

set.text: m halves 4 times = log2(16) = log2(log2 n)
